judgments.reasoning_cat1: The granting language is standard, though 'approximately 10.89 acres' and the transcription slips ('parcel!', 'any and ail', 'made apart hereof') leave minor slack about what is conveyed and rely wholly on Exhibit A. The catch-all 'all rights, privileges, easements and appurtenances, if any, thereunto belonging' is a general phrase riding on enumerated specifics, but its reach is conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The grant of interests in the beds of adjoining streets sits alongside Sections 3 and 5, which contemplate that Sixth and Abbott Streets will be vacated and new legal descriptions created, so what Exhibit A describes may not match what is finally conveyed. Section 1's assignment to Buyer of awards for change of grade also sits uneasily with Section 12, which gives condemnation awards to Seller on termination.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause twice refers to 'deductions identified below' and 'setoffs as described below' when no deductions or setoffs are in fact described anywhere, and it mixes an illustrative TIF example with the operative payment formula, leaving the timing and source of the $1,000,000 Outstanding Balance genuinely uncertain. The interest sentence ('to the same extent, if any, that either or both the City... pay interest... on the outstanding incurred eligible expenses') is opaque on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 28 repeats the last sentence but says 'less any setoff' where Section 2 says 'less any deductions', and Section 8(a)(i) says the whole 'Purchase Price, plus or minus prorations' is to be paid to Seller at Closing, which contradicts the deferred $1,000,000 mechanism here. No other provision supplies the missing schedule of deductions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The deed must convey title 'free from any and all liens or encumbrances' yet 'subject only to' Permitted Exceptions defined by reference to an Option Agreement whose date is left blank, so the defining document is not identified. 'New legal descriptions which reflect the City of Detroit's final approved plat of vacation' makes the deed depend on a municipal act that may never occur.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4 speaks of 'those Permitted Exceptions attached hereto' and the attachment list includes 'Exhibit B — Permitted Exceptions', while this section defines Permitted Exceptions by reference to the Option Agreement instead; the two sources may not coincide. Section 8(a)(ii) adds a further category ('exceptions created or suffered by Buyer') not contemplated here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The cure mechanic is garbled: Seller 'shall have ten (10) business days prior to the date of Closing' to cure is not a workable period, and Buyer must elect 'prior to the expiration of the period for Seller to remedy' — a period that is itself undefined. Blank spaces ('the office in ____') and 'expanse' for 'expense' add mechanical defects.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The reference to 'Permitted Exceptions attached hereto' conflicts with Section 3, which defines them by reference to the unattached Option Agreement. The thirty-day delivery deadline also has to be reconciled with Section 8(a)'s ninety-day outside closing date and Section 17's time-is-of-the-essence clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The obligation has no deadline and is conditioned only on execution, while its content depends on 'the City of Detroit's final approved plat of vacation and dedication of right of way' that may not exist; 'as a prepared in accordance with' is a mechanical slip. Whether Seller must procure the City's approval or merely reflect it if given is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It runs in parallel with Section 3's deed obligation, which depends on the same municipal approval, and with Section 8(a)'s ninety-day closing deadline, creating a possible impossibility if the City has not acted. Nothing elsewhere allocates responsibility for obtaining the vacation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The as-is acceptance is broad and qualified only in its middle sentence by 'except as expressly set forth elsewhere in the Agreement', leaving unclear whether the first and third sentences are similarly qualified. 'All faults of every kind and nature whatsoever whether latent or patent and whether now or hereafter existing' is sweeping and one-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits directly against Section 7(d) and 7(e) environmental representations and against Section 11, under which Seller bears risk of loss and must repair injury 'beyond the ordinary wear and tear' before deed delivery. Harmonising an unqualified acceptance of the closing-date condition with Seller's repair duty is a genuine tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare introductory lead-in; the only wrinkle is that it labels the following items both 'covenants' and 'represents', which can matter for remedy. Standing alone there is little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the closing warranty paragraph that follows and with Section 23's no-merger/survival rule. No conflicting provision identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite representation of record ownership and authority with no ambiguous term. Nothing in the wording invites competing readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the recitals identifying 1200 6th Street LLC as Seller and Section 3's covenant to convey; the only friction is Section 24's reference to the Option Agreement assigned to Buyer, which does not contradict ownership. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No knowledge of any reason why the local governmental authorities would not allow the Property to be developed for the Federal Office facilities contemplated herein' turns on an undefined project scope and a knowledge qualifier that is unqualified as to whom and how diligent. 'Possession has been peaceable and undisturbed' is an absolute statement embedded among knowledge-qualified ones.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 'Federal Office facilities contemplated herein' are nowhere described except obliquely in Section 13's 'leasehold for Federal facilities', so the representation's referent depends on an outside procurement. Section 6's as-is acknowledgment also cuts against reliance on this representation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Sufficient size, capacity' and 'without any special charge, assessment or apparatus for its current use' are vague, and 'for its current use' materially limits a representation made for a redevelopment transaction. The list of utilities is enumerated with no catch-all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 26 repeats the same sentence but adds 'Gas' and drops the 'for its current use' limitation, then places all utility relocation costs on Buyer — a direct inconsistency in scope between two representations of the same fact. That mismatch is the clearest Category 2 point in the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Facility' is defined by statute, but 'all environmental information that it has' is an undefined boundary (documents? oral knowledge? affiliates?). The disclosure is otherwise concrete.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly carved out of Section 7(e)'s knowledge representations and coexists with Section 6's as-is clause; whether the as-is clause defeats reliance on this disclosure is a real question, though the carve-out language mitigates it. Schedule A referenced in 7(e) is not among the listed attachments.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To the best of Seller's actual knowledge' qualifies three sub-representations of differing character, and subsection (3) is drafted as a conditional about 'any subsequent purchaser' availing itself of exemptions, which is close to unintelligible as a representation. The closing sentence about 'the exemptions include that owner's obligations' is grammatically broken.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It opens 'Except as otherwise indicated on Schedule A attached', but the attachment list identifies only Exhibit A (legal description) and Exhibit B (permitted exceptions) — there is no Schedule A. The carve-outs also have to be squared with Section 6's as-is acceptance and Section 7's continuing-truth warranty.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Will continue to be true and correct on each day hereafter' has no end date and is unqualified, which reads as an impossible perpetual warranty rather than a bring-down at closing. The phrase 'the above representations' does not say whether it captures the knowledge qualifiers in 7(e).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Section 23 (no merger; survival 'until fulfilled, up to and including... written acceptance of occupancy'), the survival period is stated two different ways — perpetual here, project-completion-bounded there. Section 6's as-is clause pulls in yet another direction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The provision is visibly mangled: empty subparagraph markers '(i) (ii) (iii) (iv)' precede a single obligation, so the numbering does not match the text that follows. 'A mutually agreeable date' with a ninety-day outside limit is otherwise definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The payment obligation ('the Purchase Price, plus or minus prorations') conflicts with Section 2, under which only $8,000,000 is payable at Closing and $1,000,000 is deferred against TIF receipts. The broken numbering also produces the mis-citation of 'Section 8(a)(v)' in the following subsection.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite; the only soft phrase is 'exceptions created or suffered by Buyer', which has a settled conveyancing meaning. Nothing else invites competing readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3 requires title 'free from any and all liens or encumbrances, subject only to' Permitted Exceptions, whereas this subsection adds Buyer-created exceptions — a small enlargement of what the deed may be subject to. The mismatch is modest but real.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The FIRPTA certification tracks statutory defined terms and has no vague operative language. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 8(a) and 8(b) generally; no other provision addresses foreign-person status. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such other documentation as is reasonably required by the Title Company... including, without limitation, ALTA statements and GAP undertakings' is a general catch-all against specifics, and it is then capped by the undefined term 'extraordinary obligations'. 'If required the Title Company' is missing a word.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The clause calls itself 'Section 8(a)(v)' but appears as the fourth item, while Section 8(a)(v) is the possession subsection — a cross-reference that points to the wrong provision. That misnumbering flows from the broken enumeration in Section 8(a).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, unambiguous in substance, though it does not say in what condition or free of what occupancies possession is delivered. Very little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is numbered (v) while the preceding subsection calls itself 8(a)(v), so the two compete for the same designation; substantively it fits Section 6's acceptance of the closing-date condition. Minor numbering conflict only.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional escrow-closing and fee-splitting provision with definite allocations. 'Undertakings... necessary for the Closing in escrow to occur' is mildly open-ended but standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to 'delivery of the Title Policy' though Section 4 contemplates either a policy 'or title commitment therefore', a small mismatch; otherwise it sits comfortably with Section 8(a). Section 8(a)(iv)'s bar on 'extraordinary obligations' limits the undertakings required here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All real estate taxes, expenses and charges in connection with ownership and use of the Property' is a broad, unbounded category with no proration date convention stated. What counts as an 'expense or charge in connection with... use' is genuinely open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2 already provides for 'standard deductions and prorations (customary closing expenses incurred by the Seller inclusive of utility and real estate tax prorations)', and Section 26 puts all utility relocation costs on Buyer — three overlapping cost allocations that must be harmonised. The overlap with Section 2 is the most direct.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Buyer-default remedy is internally contradictory: Seller is 'entitled to, as liquidated damages not to exceed $50,000, either a $50,000 letter of credit or cash equivalent', and the same paragraph then says 'the parties may seek any other remedy available at law or in equity', so whether the $50,000 is an exclusive cap is unresolved. 'Award and Assignment of the Option to Purchase', 'Any subsequent Buyer', and the revocation sentence are undefined and sit oddly with the five-day cure structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The liquidated-damages cap collides with the final sentence and with Section 21's fee-shifting, and the letter-of-credit obligation refers to an Assignment of the Option handled in Section 24 but nowhere else made an obligation of this Agreement. Section 17's time-is-of-the-essence clause also sits against a five-day post-notice cure right.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Injury beyond the ordinary wear and tear' and 'an appropriate deduction from the purchase price' are both vague, and the repair-or-deduct election is not clearly given to either party. The stray semicolon after 'improvements' is a minor mechanical flaw.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It contradicts Section 6, under which Buyer accepts the Property 'in the condition existing on the date of closing... including all faults... whether now or hereafter existing', and the deduction remedy has to be squared with the fixed price mechanics of Section 2. Section 12 separately handles condemnation, leaving the boundary between the two.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Substantial' is defined circularly as a portion that 'would impair or otherwise affect the intended use', and 'otherwise affect' has no boundary; the first sentence is also a fragment with a period where a comma belongs, so the trigger and the consequence are grammatically severed. 'Intended use of the Real Property' uses a term not otherwise defined in the Agreement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1 assigns to Buyer Seller's interest in awards for street takings and changes of grade, whereas this section gives all awards to Seller if Buyer terminates. 'Real Property' appears nowhere else, where the defined term is 'Property'.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is written in option-agreement language — 'during the period of this Option including any extension periods', 'Optionee', 'Optionor' — inside a purchase and sale agreement that has no option period and no such defined parties. 'Any other due diligence matters deemed reasonably prudent' is an open catch-all after an enumerated list.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The whole instrument defines only 'Seller' and 'Buyer' (recitals and Section 1), so Optionor/Optionee and 'the period of this Option' can only be reconciled by importing the Real Estate Option Agreement referenced in Sections 3 and 24. It also sits against Section 6, in which Buyer acknowledges it has already completed its investigation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Buyer's notice address is left entirely blank, and the deemed-receipt sentence covers mail and courier but not the personal delivery option expressly permitted. Whether the GSA 'copy to' is a condition of effective notice is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The blank Buyer address interacts with Sections 4, 10 and 12, all of which make written notice the trigger for termination rights and cure periods, so the mechanic on which those provisions depend is incomplete. Section 24 makes GSA a necessary signatory to amendments, which does not explain its notice role here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The representation reads 'no commission... is payable to any other person or entity', where 'other' has no antecedent because no broker is named — a small mechanical oddity that could be read as excluding a party's own broker. Otherwise short and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision addresses brokerage or indemnity for broker claims, so nothing contradicts it. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such other acts... as may be reasonably necessary' is a standard further-assurances formula whose vagueness is inherent but rarely operative on its own. Little concrete to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps with Section 8(a)(iv)'s further-documentation duty, which is capped by the 'extraordinary obligations' limit that does not appear here; the overlap is mild rather than contradictory. Section 28's cooperation duty is similar in kind.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard time-is-of-the-essence wording with a clear business-day extension rule; 'every provision hereof in which time is an element' is broad but conventional. Little ambiguity in the words themselves.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is hard to apply to a document whose date is blank and whose Closing date is only 'a mutually agreeable date' within ninety days (Section 8(a)), and it cuts against the five-day cure periods in Section 10 and the open-ended Section 5 survey duty. Those tensions are real but modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A boilerplate headings clause with settled meaning and no vague term. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It would only matter if a heading conflicted with text; Section 26's heading ('Utilities/Utilities Relocations and Costs') is broader than Section 7(c)'s, but the clause resolves rather than creates that problem. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Pure number-and-gender boilerplate; definite and self-contained. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision turns on singular/plural usage in a contested way. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The laws of the state in which the Property is located' is indirect but unambiguous given Section 1 (Detroit, Michigan); 'permitted assigns' implies an assignment consent requirement that appears nowhere. That implication is the only soft edge.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Agreement contains no assignment clause, yet Section 24 and Section 10 both contemplate assignment of the Option by GSA and 'any subsequent Buyer', so what makes an assign 'permitted' is unstated. A federal-instrumentality purchaser also raises a question about state-law construction that the clause does not address.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Prevailing party, as determined by the court' is self-defining and the recovery is limited to costs and reasonable fees. Little ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits alongside Section 10's liquidated-damages cap of $50,000, raising a question whether fees may be added to that cap, but the clauses are not squarely opposed. Otherwise consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite: amendments must be written and 'executed by each party hereto', with counterparts permitted. Nothing vague in isolation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 24's final sentence requires amendments to be 'executed by the Buyer, Seller and the Government, acting by GSA', which is a different and stricter rule than 'each party hereto' since the Government is not a party to this Agreement. That is a direct conflict between two operative provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Remain in effect until fulfilled, up to and including the time of completion of any improvements to be built thereon and the written acceptance of occupancy' fixes survival by reference to construction and occupancy events that this Agreement does not govern or define. Whether 'until fulfilled' and the occupancy date are alternatives or cumulative is unclear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states a different survival horizon from Section 7's closing warranty that the representations 'will continue to be true and correct on each day hereafter', and it depends on improvements and a GSA occupancy acceptance found only in the separate Option/lease arrangements referenced in Sections 13 and 24. Reconciling the two survival formulas is a genuine problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause says the Agreement 'cancels and supersedes all prior agreements' and 'is entire in itself' while simultaneously preserving the Real Estate Option Agreement (whose date is left blank) as an equally operative document, so the integration is self-contradictory on its face. 'No promises... other than those expressly contained herein' then refers back only to this Agreement, not the Option.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its amendment sentence requires GSA's execution, contradicting Section 22's 'executed by each party hereto', and its preservation of the Option is what makes Sections 3 (Permitted Exceptions), 10 (Award and Assignment of the Option) and 13 (Optionor/Optionee) intelligible — or not. This is the hinge provision for whole-instrument coherence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One short prohibition, definite in scope and with no vague term. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No provision elsewhere grants a recording right or requires a memorandum; Section 3's deed is separate. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The representation is a near-copy of Section 7(c) but adds 'Gas' and drops 'for its current use', and the cost sentence uses 'terminations, and relocations' with a stray comma and the intruded page number ('after 8 closing'). 'All public and quasi-public and private utilities' places an unbounded cost obligation on Buyer.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The two utility representations (this and Section 7(c)) differ in scope for no stated reason, and the allocation of all relocation costs to Buyer is in tension with the representation that utilities are available 'without any special charge, assessment or apparatus' and with Section 9's proration of 'expenses and charges in connection with ownership and use'. That duplication-with-variation is the clearest inconsistency here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard counterparts language; 'any one of which shall be considered an original' is settled. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 22 already contains a counterparts sentence for amendments, so the two overlap without contradicting. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Will cooperate with the Buyer to secure all necessary government approvals' is an undefined effort standard with no deadline or cost allocation, and 'the tax incremental reimbursement shall belong to the Buyer' is stated without identifying which reimbursement or when title to it passes. 'Less any setoff' introduces a term the Agreement never defines.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the final sentence of Section 2 but with 'less any setoff' in place of 'less any deductions', and Section 2 conditions Seller's remaining $1,000,000 on Buyer's receipt of the same TIF proceeds this section awards to Buyer. The two provisions must be read together to know who gets what and neither supplies the promised list of setoffs or deductions.
